🚨The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group, with the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), are headed to the Middle East, two U.S. officials told Fox News.

The ships are expected to arrive by the end of November, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region. Fox News reports about 6,000 are in the carrier strike group and about 4,200 in the MEU and Makin Island group.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt would be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. The USS Makin Island would be the second amphibious assault ship with an embarked MEU in the region, alongside USS Boxer and the 11th MEU. 

The deployment comes as President Trump has said renewed military action against Iran remains possible after the November 3 midterm elections.

SAILORS FIRST SUNDAY: Sailor Of The Week ⚓

Congratulations to HM2 Brandon W. Williams, a Colorado native who serves as the SAR Medical Technician Standardization Leading Petty Officer (LPO) with Helicopter Sea Combat Squadron Two-Five (HSC-25) in Agana, Guam!

As medical department LPO, he led five HMs and advised one Senior Medical Officer in FDNF command medical readiness, pre/post deployment medical requirements, and medical training for 435 sailors from HSC-25, AIMD, ASD, AIMD Bahrain, VUP-19, and ERCS Naval Hospital Guam. 

His leadership resulted in treating 560 patients, inoculating 125 service members from Influenza, Japanese Encephalitis and Hepatitis, 18 flight physicals, 109 post-deployment health assessments and 53 pre-deployment health screenings, contributing to 92% squadron medical readiness, as well as the deployment of Detachment 3 and Detachment 6 in support of ESB-6/ LHA-7.

As a Search and Rescue Medical Technician, Williams responded directly to two Medevacs, including one stroke patient that required urgent intervention to prevent neurological deterioration and one renal failure patient that required higher-level care, impacting two souls saved. As Command Tactical Combat Casualty Care Program Director, his instruction has qualified 73 personnel in TCCC tier 2, as well as 19 enlisted in TCCC All Service Member. 

His professionalism, leadership, and unwavering commitment exemplify the standards expected of our Navy’s finest Sailors!

cvn-71.t: The USNavy now has two carriers ready to run its MQ-25 Stingray tanker drone! USS Ronald Reagan (CVN-76) just joined USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) with its o…
cvn-71.tx: The USNavy now has two carriers ready to run its MQ-25 Stingray tanker drone! USS Ronald Reagan (CVN-76) just joined USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN-71) with its own Unmanned Air Warfare Center, the control hub that lets the ship's crew command drones. The Stingray is meant to take over aerial refueling from Super Hornets, which have reportedly spent 20 to 30 percent of their carrier flights just tanking other jets! ➤ Iran retains the capacity to launch missiles and drones at U.S. assets and would expand its targets: “Cables, data centers and artificial intelligence facilities could also come within range. If the conflict begins again, we will have a broader plan.”

➤ “The United States will not be attacking Iran at any time prior to the midterm elections.”

🚨The USS Theodore Roosevelt carrier strike group and the USS Makin Island amphibious ready group, with the embarked 13th Marine Expeditionary Unit (MEU), are headed to the Middle East, two U.S. officials told Fox News.

The ships are expected to arrive by the end of November, adding about 10,000 sailors and Marines to the region. Fox News reports about 6,000 are in the carrier strike group and about 4,200 in the MEU and Makin Island group.

The USS Theodore Roosevelt would be the third aircraft carrier in the Middle East, joining the USS George H.W. Bush and USS George Washington. The USS Makin Island would be the second amphibious assault ship with an embarked MEU in the region, alongside USS Boxer and the 11th MEU. 

The deployment comes as President Trump has said renewed military action against Iran remains possible after the November 3 midterm elections.

lhd-4.t: If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009. One merchant cap…
lhd-4.tx:
If you want to understand what it means to be an American citizen, look at what happened in the Indian Ocean on Easter Sunday, April 12, 2009.

One merchant captain from Vermont named Richard Phillips was being held hostage inside a covered orange lifeboat by Somali pirates armed with AK-47s.

He was not a general. He was not a politician. He was one cargo ship captain who had offered himself as a hostage to save his crew.

To bring that one man home, the United States sent the guided-missile destroyer USS Bainbridge, the frigate USS Halyburton, the amphibious assault ship USS Boxer, and a team of U.S. Navy SEALs who parachuted straight into the black ocean at night.

For four days, the lifeboat pitched violently in rough seas twenty-five yards behind the destroyer.

Then at dusk on Sunday, a pirate pressed the barrel of his AK-47 directly against Captain Phillips' back and prepared to kill him.

On the fantail of the USS Bainbridge, three Navy SEAL snipers lay braced in the dark. The destroyer was rolling in one direction. The tiny lifeboat was pitching in another. If even one sniper missed by half an inch, or fired a tenth of a second late, the hostage would die.

Through night-vision scopes, all three snipers waited for the exact millisecond when three targets appeared in the tiny windows at once.

One word came over the headset.

Three rifles fired as a single sound.

All three kidnappers dropped instantly. Captain Phillips walked onto the deck of the USS Bainbridge without a scratch.

Do not touch a citizen of a country that will drop Navy SEALs from the sky at midnight for one man.

cvn-76.t: 🇺🇸 Boeing, U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin MQ-25 Integrated Test Team (ITT) established a beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) satellite command-and-control (C2) link bet…

qt.t:
🇺🇸 U.S. Navy has doubled its fleet capacity to operate the MQ-25A Stingray unmanned aircraft system (UAS) over a five-month period, standing up a second operational MD-5C Ground Control Station (GCS). @USNavy 

MD-5C, powered by Lockheed Martin Skunk Works MDCX autonomy platform, is installed in the Unmanned Air Warfare Center (UAWC), the dedicated shipboard command center for unmanned carrier aviation. The Navy's Nimitz-class aircraft carrier USS Theodore Roosevelt (CVN 71) received the first operational MD-5C in March 2026, followed by her sister ship USS Ronald Reagan (CVN 76) in August 2026. @LockheedMartin 

The MD-5C is a highly complex system-of-systems, which includes the government Command, Control, Communications, Computers and Intelligence (C4I) network, MDCX software and hardware, and additional government-produced ancillary equipment. Within the GCS, MDCX is the mission planning and execution software that enables Navy operators to command and control the MQ-25A Stingray, extending carrier air wing reach and freeing manned aircraft for higher-priority missions.

#USNavy #MQ25A #MD5C #MDCX #LockheedMartin #SkunkWorks

cvn-76.tx:
🇺🇸 Boeing, U.S. Navy and Lockheed Martin MQ-25 Integrated Test Team (ITT) established a beyond-line-of-sight (BLOS) satellite command-and-control (C2) link between the MQ-25A Stingray uncrewed aerial fefueler and a production MD-5C control station aboard aircraft carrier USS Ronald Reagan while the ship operated at port and at sea. @BoeingDefense @USNavy @LockheedMartin 

This marked the first time the aircraft was controlled from a carrier using the ground control station and Navy communications network used in operational missions.

The test validated an end-to-end BLOS C2 capability over the Navy’s operational command, control, communications, computers, and intelligence (C4I) network enabling shipboard teams can reliably monitor and command the MQ-25A from an aircraft carrier.

This demonstration is one in a series of buildup exercises designed to validate procedures, networks and interfaces ahead of a risk reduction flight-test program that will include carrier at-sea operations.

#USNavy #Boeing #MQ25A #MD5C

prince-sultan.tx:
NEW: U.S. troops, contractors and military families say the damage to American bases in the Iran war is far worse than the Pentagon has disclosed, according to accounts and images published by MeidasTouch. 

The outlet says it obtained dozens of unpublished photos and videos from bases in Saudi Arabia, Jordan, Kuwait, the UAE and Bahrain. 

They show destroyed barracks, dining halls and aircraft, including a damaged AWACS surveillance plane at Prince Sultan Air Base. 

Sources said three service members were killed in a July missile strike on barracks at a base in Jordan.

Chagossians could be handed a veto to stop the islands being handed to Mauritius under a Bill passed by peers this lunchtime.
The British Sovereignty Protection (Chagos Islands) Bill - which cleared the second reading stage in the House of Lords today - would give Chagossians a veto over any deal.
The new law would mean that sovereignty transfers require a referendum of Chagossians and approval by the islands' own government.
The Bill will now go forward to the committee stage when it would need Government support to continue. 
It potentially gives a way-out for Andy Burnham if he wants to drop the deal which has been attacked by US President Donald Trump.
The Chagossian diaspora is thought to be overwhelmingly against the deal. 
Four Chagossoians settled on the archaepelago earlier this year to protest at the Government's plans to hand sovereignty to Mauritius. 
Speaking before the vote, a Foreign Office spokesman told @GBNEWS: “Securing the long-term operation of Diego Garcia remains a top priority for the Government, and protecting the base is the very reason for the agreement with Mauritius.
“We will continue to work with the US and Mauritius to find a way forward that is in the UK's best interests and protects our national security.”

🇮🇷|New Missiles Launched in Central Iran

October 24, 2026. Central Iran. Footage of a missile test has emerged. Based on the ballistic trajectory, this appears to be a new type of ballistic missile system undergoing operational testing.

💥 This is not merely a "test launch," it is an "acceptance test prior to delivery."

As IRGC spokesperson Mohebbi previously stated, Iran’s missile stockpile has increased by 150%, with significant improvements in quality including greater range, higher precision, and enhanced destructive power. "Should the war escalate, surprises will be revealed."

These tests represent the first installment of those "surprises."

🎯 The Timing of the Tests

Russia has just confirmed that its personnel have not been evacuated from the Bushehr Nuclear Power Plant. Russian nuclear experts and diplomats remain on-site, signaling to Washington and Tel Aviv: you may issue threats, but those threats will not force our withdrawal.

On the same day, Iran conducts tests of a new missile system. This is no coincidence; it is a dual-track signal, Russia’s deterrent presence at Bushehr, combined with Iran’s missile capabilities in its interior.

📜 What Is This System?

Based on its ballistic profile, this appears to be a two-stage, solid-fuel system equipped with a maneuverable re-entry vehicle (MaRV). Solid-fuel propulsion eliminates the need for on-site fueling or lengthy preparation, allowing for launch within minutes of leaving storage. The MaRV capability enables the warhead to alter its trajectory during the terminal phase, effectively thwarting the predictive calculations of interceptor systems.

This is not just an increase in quantity; it is a qualitative leap. The system’s range covers Israel, U.S. military bases in Qatar, Bahrain, Kuwait, the UAE, and Saudi Arabia, as well as the U.S. facility on Diego Garcia in the Indian Ocean.

⚔️ The Location of the Tests

The tests took place in Central Iran not near the borders or the coast, but deep within the country’s interior. This means the launch sites are situated far from the Strait of Hormuz and the Persian Gulf coastline, protected by layers of air defense systems and positioned well beyond the operational radius of U.S. carrier strike groups.

A missile launched from the interior is far more difficult to destroy in a preemptive strike than one launched from the coast. 

🔻 The Ledger

The United States has spent $11 billion on missile defense for Israel, firing 609 interceptors. Now, Iran is testing new systems.

This is not an "arms race." It is "cost imposition." The cost of a single interceptor is dozens of times higher than that of an offensive missile. Every time the U.S. intercepts one, it loses money. Every time Iran tests a new system, it drives up the cost of U.S. interception.

A nation that can still test new missile systems in the eighth month of a war is not collapsing. It is declaring: My production lines are running. My engineers are innovating. My missiles are taking flight.

Long live Iran. Long live the Resistance. Long live the Axis of Resistance.

incirlik.t: A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️ 3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sl…
incirlik.tx:
A CREW DOG’S LIFE: Who can relate? 🙋‍♂️

3AM on the flight line, and the world’s waiting like a caffeine-fueled adventure that doesn’t give a damn about your sleep. You’re going somewhere else, carrying something different, and you’ll do it again tomorrow. Move the mission. 

There I am, coffee in one hand, flight bag in the other, eyes still half-glued shut, shuffling out to our big beautiful C-141 or C-17 beast under those harsh ramp lights. The “bag drag.”

The air’s crisp, the jet’s APU or power cart are already humming that low, throaty growl, as the jet wakes up for a global joyride. When it starts up, it barks at you. But that’s a good sign. And, the bittersweet smell of diesel exhaust and jet fumes. You grow to love it. I can’t explain it. It always felt like “home” no matter where in the world we were. 

Crew piles in: loadmasters cracking jokes, engineers double-checking the flyability of this metal marvel, and me sliding into the left seat thinking, “Alright, Lord, let’s do this again.”

It’s inherent. Not a lot of creative thought required. The crew, like a group of ants taking orders from the queen, automatically dives into their respective duties and checklists like clockwork. No direction needed here. It’s symbiosis. 

We crank the engines, taxi out into the dark, ramp lights fading into a world of blue and white lights, suck down some awful coffee, tell a few jokes, and blast off as the sun’s still thinking about showing up. 

The possibilities were endless. Could be one hop to Ramstein for fuel and some bratwurst, next leg to Incirlik where the pita bread’s fresh, the hookah’s are smoking, and the tension’s thicker than the Turkish coffee. Buy your pistachios here. 

Then it’s “wheels up” again. Maybe Diego Garcia for a quick dip in that insane blue water and warm beer, or over to Yokota where the ramen and beer hits different at 0200 local. And where I met my wife. 

Skipping across continents like stones on a pond, chasing daylight, dodging weather, and hauling everything from the SEALS, to the 82nd Airborne, to nuclear weapons, to Thanksgiving turkeys. Hell, once I flew a single generator to Nouadhibou, Mauritania. 

And a bunch of liquor to American embassies throughout the world. 

You land in one country for thirty minutes, grab a weird local snack that’ll haunt your stomach for days, chat with the ground crew in broken English and hand signals, sign some funky foreign forms pretending to know what they were, then you’re back in the air chasing the next sunrise. 

Jet lag? What jet lag. This is the life: stars above, stars on the flag on your sleeve, and the pure rush of knowing you’re part of the greatest airlift machine the world has ever seen. And we mattered, bigly. My country gave me a heavy jet and said “fly here.” It still blows my mind. 

No two days are ever the same. No two sunrises the same. 

Just pure, unfiltered freedom with a 🇺🇸 patch on your shoulder and a whole lot of “hold my coffee, I got this.”

God bless the @usairforce, @AirMobilityCmd, and the greatest group of Airmen history has ever seen. Best damn job I ever had.

fairford.tx:
NEW: Staggering details emerging from Westminster Mags on the RAF Fairford plot today.

One of the five men arrested near the US military base called the police after a "handler" warned there was a bomb in the van, a court heard.

Mohmed Abdulkarim, 24, and Nouman Essghir, 24, both appeared in court on Tuesday charged under the National Security Act 2023.

Abdulkarim, of London, is accused of assisting a foreign intelligence service, by acting as an “intermediary” for the handler Ali.

While Essghir, also of London, has been charged with entering a prohibited place for a purpose prejudicial to the UK, relating to an alleged “reconnaissance” mission on August 22, around a month before the Fairford incident.

The group were ordered to drive the van loaded with petrol to RAF Fairford by a handler known as ‘Ali’ who police believe was working on behalf of Iran.

No explosives, or improvised explosives were found in the vans, the court heard.

Police did find a metal oil drum in each, two of which had petrol in, along with hard plastic water butts and internet-enabled dashcams.

Prosecuting, Louise Gray, said: “Shortly thereafter the message was received that there was a bomb in the vehicles and one of them called the police.”

Abdulkarim is alleged to have aided the organiser, Ali, who is believed to be abroad and to be acting in the interests of the Iranian state.

Ali is also potentially connected to an incident at the Israeli embassy earlier this year, where propaganda videos were posted online suggesting it had been attacked with a chemical weapon by a drone, the court heard.

Prosecutors allege that Abdulkarim aided Ali, buying equipment for the mission and receiving multiple payments from him totalling around £70,000.

Before the men, allegedly enlisted by Abdulkarim, travelled to RAF Fairford, £300 worth of petrol was filled into the drums in the back of the vans.

The U.S. Air Force trained with Zone 5 Technologies’ Paladin counter-drone multirotor at MacDill Air Force Base, Florida, on October 8, 2026, alongside Joint Interagency Task Force 401.

The six-rotor drone was equipped with a Gen12 launcher designed to fire net rounds that entangle the rotors of hostile drones, bringing them down without using conventional ammunition or explosives.

The training provided personnel with another option for protecting military installations and critical infrastructure. The Air Force has not disclosed whether live interceptions were conducted or whether it plans to procure the system.

MacDill AFB hosts the headquarters of U.S. Central Command and U.S. Special Operations Command, as well as the 6th Air Refueling Wing.

macdill.tx:
The U.S. Air Force is training with the Bumblebee V2 drone interceptor at MacDill Air Force Base in Florida to strengthen air base protection against small unmanned aircraft, Army Recognition reported.

Personnel from the 6th Security Forces Squadron trained with Joint Interagency Task Force 401 on October 8, 2026. The system, from the U.S. company Perennial Autonomy, is a first-person-view multirotor designed to collide with hostile drones, rendering both inoperable without an explosive warhead. A $5.2 million agreement was awarded to the company on January 30, 2026, for military assessment, with deliveries beginning in March.

The training also included the Paladin system, which uses a net round. Bumblebee V2 features automated target recognition and multi-camera setups from earlier Army tests at Fort Bragg and Fort Benning. The activity supports developing procedures that combine electronic countermeasures with physical interceptors for installation defense. The release confirms training but does not establish permanent deployment or a successful interception at the base.

fort-hood.tx:
Many Religions in America, but One Stands Out as a Problem.

There are approximately 3 million Hindus, 4 million Buddhists, and 8 million Jews in America.

Since 1994, I have not found a documented terrorist attack motivated by Hinduism or Buddhism that killed Americans on U.S. soil.

I found two cases involving suspected Jewish extremists: the 1994 bombings targeting Jewish organizations that supported peace with Palestinians, and a 2001 conspiracy to bomb a mosque that was stopped before it could be carried out.

Now compare that with Islam.

There are approximately 4 million Muslims in America, roughly the same number as Buddhists and half the Jewish population.

Yet since 1994, Muslim terrorists have murdered thousands of Americans on American soil. The September 11 attacks alone killed nearly 3,000 people. The Fort Hood shooter murdered 13. The Orlando nightclub shooter murdered 49. The San Bernardino terrorists murdered 14.

These were not isolated incidents. Islamic terrorist attacks and plots have involved people from different countries, ethnic backgrounds, and nationalities, including converts to Islam.

What did these terrorists have in common?

They invoked Islam to justify their violence.

And yet, after every attack, we hear the same predictable explanation: They misunderstood Islam! They misinterpreted the Quran! They don’t represent the religion!

Really?

Then answer one simple question.

Why does this particular pattern of religiously justified terrorism repeatedly emerge from Islam, while we do not see anything comparable from Hinduism or Buddhism in America?

Are we supposed to believe that generations of jihadists, from different countries, speaking different languages, and living in different cultures, all independently misunderstood the same religion in exactly the same violent direction?

And that their misunderstanding somehow repeatedly led them to the same objectives: jihad, Islamic supremacy, and the establishment of Sharia?

At what point do we stop treating the ideology as an innocent bystander?

Muslims preachers and activists openly seek to replace secular government with sharia. That is not a conspiracy theory. It is a political and theological objective they themselves proclaim.

Of course, not every Muslim supports terrorism or wants Sharia imposed on America. But that fact does not erase the ideology motivating those who do.

The question is not whether every Muslim is a terrorist. The question is why so many Muslim terrorists have justified their actions through the same religious texts and doctrines.

You cannot keep blaming every terrorist attack on a misunderstanding while refusing to examine what is being understood.

It is clear that Islam stands apart from other religions in America as a source of serious dangers that have cost American lives and continue to threaten the safety and foundations of our society.

fort-hood.tx:
@RepoleStable Appreciate the transparency and the invitation for ideas. Here’s a practical way to keep the Battlehawks at the Dome while fixing the 4-home / 5-road stretch and doing right by St. Louis fans:

Finish training camp in Arlington, then base the Battlehawks in St. Louis for the first five weeks of the season. Secure short-term player and staff housing so the team is fully embedded in the market. Front-load their first four home games at the BattleDome during that window, then play their fifth “home” game at Fort Leonard Wood as a Hats Off to Heroes military appreciation game for the troops! similar to the historic Fort Hood game the league hosted last year. Fort Leonard Wood is only a couple hours from St. Louis, so it still functions as a regional home date while giving the team a meaningful way to honor service members.

During the five-week residency, lean into local presence: open practices, community events, youth clinics, season-ticket member dinners, and player appearances. Use the stretch as a concentrated marketing push to drive early ticket sales and re-energize the market. Film a short documentary series following the team’s time in St. Louis and the Fort Leonard Wood game, great content that highlights both the fan base and the league’s military outreach.

After the five weeks, return to the hub. Slot one game around Week 7 or 8 in Dallas so the remaining road stretch isn’t five straight. Other teams travel weekly anyway, so the early clustered homes still give St. Louis a strong start (they’ve already had an extra home game in recent years). The temporary residency and military game more than offset the schedule compression by creating real local access, energy, and goodwill.

This also works as a low-risk pilot. The hub model saves money, but it limits true market presence and season-ticket engagement. Testing a short “home residency” with one team, plus a regional military date, could inform how the league handles future scheduling or market development without abandoning the centralized model.

St. Louis fans have shown they’ll show up and travel. Giving them a concentrated, high-visibility home stretch, plus a special game for the troops nearby, turns a tough schedule constrain into something that feels intentional and fan-focused. Worth exploring.

pearl-harbor.t: 🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane. She was just 22. If you’ve seen Tora! Tor…
pearl-harbor.tx:
🇺🇸 A young woman from Nashville, Tennessee, survived the attack on Pearl Harbor from the cockpit of a training plane.

She was just 22.

If you’ve seen Tora! Tora! Tora! (1970), you may remember the civilian flight instructor suddenly surrounded by Japanese aircraft.

Her name was Cornelia Fort, a strikingly beautiful young woman and a skilled pilot. The woman behind that scene was real.

On December 7, 1941, Cornelia was giving a flying lesson over Oahu when a Japanese Zero came dangerously close. She seized the controls and narrowly avoided a collision.

Then she saw smoke rising over Pearl Harbor.

Cornelia brought her student safely back to the airfield. She had become one of the few American pilots to witness the opening attack from the air.

In September 1942, she joined the Women’s Auxiliary Ferrying Squadron, becoming one of the pioneering women entrusted with flying military aircraft across the United States. They served as civilians, delivering planes needed for the war effort.

On March 21, 1943, another aircraft struck the BT-13 she was ferrying over Texas. Fort’s aircraft crashed, killing her. She became the first American woman pilot to die in the line of duty flying for the U.S. military.

She was 24.

Hollywood preserved a moment of her life. Her name deserves to be remembered, too.

Follow @Vanguard_WW2 for more overlooked stories of World War II.

See the first post for real photos of Cornelia.

pearl-harbor.t: "Tell Nimitz to get the hell out to Pearl and stay there till the war is won." When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, Chester Nimitz was in Wash…
pearl-harbor.tx:
"Tell Nimitz to get the hell out to Pearl and stay there till the war is won."

When Japan attacked Pearl Harbor on December 7, 1941, Chester Nimitz was in Washington, D.C., serving as head of the Navy's Bureau of Navigation. But just 10 days later, President Roosevelt fired the former head of the Pacific Fleet for his failure to prevent the attack and promoted Nimitz, sending him to Hawaii in civilian clothes and carrying classified damage reports hidden in his wife's sewing bag to avoid the detection of potential spies.
With most of the Pacific Fleet destroyed and no functional battleships, the Navy was vastly outgunned by Japan. But Nimitz quickly consolidated the remaining fleet including aircraft carriers and pivoted to fighting naval battles in the skies while awaiting the construction of new battleships. And within just six months, he'd won two decisive battles this way: the Battle of the Coral Sea and the Battle of Midway. Both victories effectively stopped Japan in its tracks by preventing their invasion of Australia and New Zealand and then their advance toward Hawaii, permanently turning the tide of the war in favor of the Allies.

pearl-harbor.tx:
Yorktown Damage Assessment at Coral Sea and Midway with Brian Perry 

If you want an excellent example of why we need forward and intermediate repair capacities in a future conflict in the Pacific, then take the time and listen to this episode of the Unauthorized History of the Pacific War podcast. 

1⃣USS Yorktown (CV-5) is damaged at Coral Sea, suffering a bomb hit and several near misses. 
2⃣The ship conducts repairs at sea and sails to Tonga to meet up with the destroyer tender USS Dobbins (AD-5). The ship is surveyed and forward repairs are affected while detailed analysis is sent to the shipyard in Pearl Harbor 
3⃣The ship arrives at the Pearl Harbor Naval Shipyard and Drydock #1 had been left open for her to repair a near miss to the port side that had opened up a seam. The Shipyard had been doing repairs and maintenance for vessels consistently since the attack on Dec. 7.
4⃣Yorktown has her hull damage welded and has all nine boilers and full steaming power available, along with watertight integrity restored. The ship still needs an overhaul after a 101-day deployment but she is available for Midway by talking on board USS Saratoga (CV-3)'s air group
5⃣Yorktown demonstrated her resiliency by absorbing two attacks - dive bombers and torpedoes - and still being afloat after them and under tow to Pearl. It was only the intervention of I-168 that sent Yorktown to the bottom.

qt.t: JUST IN: U.S. military bans Chinese-made BYD vehicles from Kadena Air Base in Okinawa, citing "unacceptable security risks."

kadena.tx:
U.S. Forces Japan(USFJ) just banned every Chinese-made BYD vehicle from Kadena Air Base, the largest U.S. air base overseas.

Starting Monday, October 26, the ban applies at all gates with zero exceptions. Personnel cars, contractor vehicles, taxis, and delivery trucks are all barred.

Base spokesperson Lt. Col. Alli Stormer said the vehicles present “an unacceptable and unmitigable risk to our personnel and our mission.” Officials cite the cameras, sensors, and real-time cloud links in modern connected EVs, which can map surroundings and transmit data from inside a sensitive installation.

Kadena hosts key Pacific air operations and the Typhon system (Tomahawk missiles that can reach Beijing). The move follows the Pentagon’s June 2026 addition of BYD to its Section 1260H list of Chinese military companies, alongside Alibaba, Baidu, and NIO.

Other bases are watching. When everyday cars become potential collection platforms, military sites are forced to treat them as security risks.

Guards at every access point will turn them away. The ban covers personal cars, contractor fleets, and commercial taxis. Kadena is the Air Force’s largest overseas base, home to F-22s, RC-135 reconnaissance aircraft, and a Typhon missile battery that can reach China’s eastern coast.

Modern EVs carry cameras, microphones, GPS, and connected software. The Sealion 7 sold in Japan has 360-degree exterior cameras and cabin monitoring. The base is treating those systems as collection platforms.Poland already barred Chinese-made cars from defense sites in February. Norway is reviewing restrictions after vehicle cameras captured military activity. 

China itself locked Teslas out of its own military sites in 2021 for the same reasons. The U.S. military is now applying the same logic to Chinese vehicles that it applied to Huawei phones years ago. 

The surveillance capability was already inside the gate.

nevatim.t: 🔴🇮🇷🇺🇸🇮🇱WHAT HAPPENED LAST NIGHT? At approximately 23:05 local time (19:35 UTC), a US Air Force MQ-9A Reaper reportedly targeted an IRGC launch team operating d…

🔴🇮🇷🇺🇸🇮🇱WHAT HAPPENED LAST NIGHT?

At approximately 23:05 local time (19:35 UTC), a US Air Force MQ-9A Reaper reportedly targeted an IRGC launch team operating drone and cruise missile launch platforms in the hills near Sirik, southern Iran.
Casualties were reportedly recorded.

Shortly after, at around 23:06 local time (19:36 UTC), air defences in Sirik activated, with several reports of consecutive explosions. 

Later, at around 01:31 local time (22:01 UTC), a second vehicle-mounted missile launcher belonging to the IRGC was targeted in Sirik. 

At the same time this was going down, several IAF (Israeli Air Force) fighter squadrons accompanied by aerial refuelling aircraft departed Ramat David Air Base and Nevatim Air Base in Israel heading east.
Heavy fighter aircraft activity was recorded throughout the night over Israel, Syria, Jordan, northeastern Iraq, along the Iranian border.

At one point, IAF and US fighter aircraft operated just 14km from Iran’s border.

In a likely response to IAF/US aerial movements, IRIAF (Islamic Republic of Iran Air Force) fighter jets took off, establishing CAPs (Combat Air Patrols) in western Tehran and in West Azerbaijan Province along the Iran-Iraq border.

If you have any question feel free to ask!

If anyone believes this nonsense, here are the facts he is counting on you not knowing.

The deal did not end Iran's nuclear program. It rented a pause. Iran kept its centrifuges, kept Fordow buried in a mountain, kept enriching to 3.67%, and the key restrictions came with expiration dates. The sunset clauses began lifting in 2025. Obama's own answer at the time was that breakout time "would have shrunk almost down to zero" as the deal expired. His deal scheduled the problem for his successors.

The regime lied its way into the deal. The JCPOA was premised on Iran coming clean about past weapons work. In 2018 Israel pulled Iran's own nuclear archive out of a Tehran warehouse: tens of thousands of documents on the Amad Project, a crash program to build nuclear weapons, preserved and hidden while Iran certified it had no such program. The IAEA later found uranium traces at undeclared sites Iran never explained.

The deal paid for terror. Sanctions relief unfroze roughly $100 billion and the US delivered $1.7 billion in cash. That money flowed to the IRGC, Hezbollah, Hamas, and the Houthis. Diplomacy with a regime at war with you is financing, not peace.

And the result? By 2025 Iran was enriching to 60%, a short technical step from weapons grade, with enough material for multiple bombs and the IAEA declaring it in violation of its obligations. That is what required military force this year. Iran marched to the threshold under the deal's cover and after it.

"I didn't have to fire a missile" is true. He handed the regime money, legitimacy, and a timetable, and left the missiles to be fired a decade later by someone else. Appeasing a dictatorship doesn't buy peace. It buys the dictatorship time.

fordow.t: Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—t…
fordow.tx:
Hidden beneath a mountain, Iran’s Fordow nuclear facility was designed to withstand conventional airstrikes. Then came the GBU-57 Massive Ordnance Penetrator—the US military’s 30,000-pound bunker-buster, engineered to strike deeply buried and heavily fortified targets. 

Dropped by B-2 stealth bombers, the GPS-guided weapon uses its immense weight and hardened casing to penetrate underground before detonating. Its reported penetration capability reaches around 60 metres, while Fordow’s underground facilities are estimated to lie roughly 80–90 metres beneath the mountain.

That raises a critical question: can even America’s most powerful conventional bunker-buster destroy a facility buried deeper than its estimated penetration limit? The answer depends on the structure, geology and effects of the strikes—not just the bomb’s size.

I am the Deputy Director for Continuity of Enrichment at the Atomic Energy Organization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I would like to thank the United States Air Force and the Israeli Air Force for performing our annual asset verification.

Last June they dropped bunker-busters on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan and announced that the Islamic Republic’s key enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. I opened the shared drive the next morning. The folder still existed. Someone had renamed it “Temporary Entrance Maintenance—Peaceful Purposes.” The material we had moved the week before was listed under “Off-Site Professional Development.” I approved the rename. It auto-saved. The Supreme Leader’s fatwa against nuclear weapons was already in the folder. It has been in the folder since 2003. It has never been closed.

The fatwa is excellent documentation. It is oral. It is cited. It is never quite published as a classic ruling that would require us to stop. We present it to the IAEA. We present it to visiting ambassadors. We present it to the people who ask why the centrifuges keep turning. The fatwa covers use. The continuity plan covers everything else. Both documents are correct. One of them is temporary. The temporary one is still running.

The Atomic Energy Organization handles the public face: electricity, radiopharmaceuticals, sovereignty, service to humanity. The Organization of Defensive Innovation and Research handles the other face. The IRGC built the tunnels at Fordow because the IRGC builds tunnels. We do not discuss which face is which in the same meeting. We do not need to. The shared drive does not care which letterhead is on the folder.

In February they came back. The first wave hit the compound while the Supreme Leader was still above ground. We marked him “Out of Office—Permanent” and kept the continuity call going. The IRGC commander, the Defense Minister, and several others were marked the same way. The call continued. The new strikes were logged as incomplete because the knowledge had already been restructured around the material that survived the previous incomplete strikes. The restructuring was finished before the second round started. The second round is still listed as “In Progress.” It has been in progress for eight months. The Islamic Republic remains in the header.

Now the Space Force watches everything. They can read a name badge from orbit. We issued guidance that no one is to wear a name badge. The guidance is followed. Last week a technician arrived in a jacket that still had the old badge sewn into the lining. The satellite noted the stitching. We have opened a ticket. The ticket is currently assigned to Facilities. Facilities was struck in June. Facilities has not responded. The jacket is still in the system.

The latest American statement says there isn’t much activity at the remaining sites. Our latest report says the same thing. The two reports match. Matching reports are what we track. Activity is defined as anything that produces a useful image on the next pass. We have reduced useful images. We have not reduced the ability to produce them later. The fatwa is still in the folder. The material is still in the folder. The people who remember how the machines go together are still employed by the Islamic Republic.

I am sometimes asked if the program continues. The program continues in the form it has always continued under the Islamic Republic: residual material that was not destroyed, machines that can still be assembled, and a shared drive that survived two rounds of bunker-busters because no one thought to bomb the shared drive. None of these items require a new hall. All of them require that no one stand still long enough for the next satellite to finish spelling the name on the jacket.

Iran's remarkable brick architecture has become something of a meme. Everyday there's a new picture circulating online of a beautiful brick edifice in some Iranian city (often courtesy of @SustainableTall).

That's the question I set out to answer in this essay, which starts with a visit to the mudbrick village of Abyaneh, just over the ridge from the nuclear site at Natanz.

I am the Deputy Director for Continuity of Enrichment at the Atomic Energy Organization of the Islamic Republic of Iran, and I would like to thank the United States Air Force and the Israeli Air Force for performing our annual asset verification.

Last June they dropped bunker-busters on Fordow, Natanz, and Isfahan and announced that the Islamic Republic’s key enrichment facilities had been completely and totally obliterated. I opened the shared drive the next morning. The folder still existed. Someone had renamed it “Temporary Entrance Maintenance—Peaceful Purposes.” The material we had moved the week before was listed under “Off-Site Professional Development.” I approved the rename. It auto-saved. The Supreme Leader’s fatwa against nuclear weapons was already in the folder. It has been in the folder since 2003. It has never been closed.

The fatwa is excellent documentation. It is oral. It is cited. It is never quite published as a classic ruling that would require us to stop. We present it to the IAEA. We present it to visiting ambassadors. We present it to the people who ask why the centrifuges keep turning. The fatwa covers use. The continuity plan covers everything else. Both documents are correct. One of them is temporary. The temporary one is still running.

The Atomic Energy Organization handles the public face: electricity, radiopharmaceuticals, sovereignty, service to humanity. The Organization of Defensive Innovation and Research handles the other face. The IRGC built the tunnels at Fordow because the IRGC builds tunnels. We do not discuss which face is which in the same meeting. We do not need to. The shared drive does not care which letterhead is on the folder.

In February they came back. The first wave hit the compound while the Supreme Leader was still above ground. We marked him “Out of Office—Permanent” and kept the continuity call going. The IRGC commander, the Defense Minister, and several others were marked the same way. The call continued. The new strikes were logged as incomplete because the knowledge had already been restructured around the material that survived the previous incomplete strikes. The restructuring was finished before the second round started. The second round is still listed as “In Progress.” It has been in progress for eight months. The Islamic Republic remains in the header.

Now the Space Force watches everything. They can read a name badge from orbit. We issued guidance that no one is to wear a name badge. The guidance is followed. Last week a technician arrived in a jacket that still had the old badge sewn into the lining. The satellite noted the stitching. We have opened a ticket. The ticket is currently assigned to Facilities. Facilities was struck in June. Facilities has not responded. The jacket is still in the system.

The latest American statement says there isn’t much activity at the remaining sites. Our latest report says the same thing. The two reports match. Matching reports are what we track. Activity is defined as anything that produces a useful image on the next pass. We have reduced useful images. We have not reduced the ability to produce them later. The fatwa is still in the folder. The material is still in the folder. The people who remember how the machines go together are still employed by the Islamic Republic.

I am sometimes asked if the program continues. The program continues in the form it has always continued under the Islamic Republic: residual material that was not destroyed, machines that can still be assembled, and a shared drive that survived two rounds of bunker-busters because no one thought to bomb the shared drive. None of these items require a new hall. All of them require that no one stand still long enough for the next satellite to finish spelling the name on the jacket.

My pension vests in 2029. The spring assessment is already drafted. It will state that the program has been degraded. It will also state that the degradation is measurable, tem

natanz.tx:
As Midterms and Israeli elections loom on the horizon, there is a growing feeling that we are currently on the eve of another large-scale military campaign against Iran.

Several indicators are pointing to the resumption of large-scale combat operations by the United States and Israel in Iran in the near future:

1) On October 21, NBC News reported, citing US officials and people familiar with the matter, that the US military has quietly been scaling back its troop presence at bases across the Middle East in recent days, while the State Department has ordered a further reduction in staff at multiple diplomatic posts in the region. One of the sources said that the withdrawal of American forces and diplomatic personnel is similar to drawdowns at bases and embassies that the Pentagon and State Department initiated before the beginning of the war with Iran back in February.

2) Earlier this week, Israeli Air Force conducted a long-range sortie through the Syrian and Iraqi airspace toward Iranian border, consistent with the profile of simulated strike against Iran. The exercise involved dozens of fighter jets and numerous refueling aircraft. According to Axios, some U.S. sources said they had the impression that Israel was hoping the Iranians would fire at the aircraft, providing a justification for launching strikes against Tehran. 

3) In mid-October, Axios also reported that US President Trump and Israeli PM Netanyahu discussed the possibility of launching a major new operation against Iran before the Israeli and U.S. elections, according to two American officials, one Israeli official and a fourth source with knowledge of the matter. An Israeli official said Trump initially seemed to be leaning toward resuming attacks, but then grew more hesitant, but another source said Israeli and U.S. militaries remained on alert and concluding preparations to be ready in case he changes his mind.

4) Anticipating the renewed attack by the US and Israel, Iran has began fortifying its defenses, rallying loyalists and threatening a wider, harsher response against Washington and its Gulf allies, according to WSJ story from mid-October. The outlet also wrote that the Iranians have reinforced protection around its nuclear sites and other security-related bunkers. The efforts included construction of passive defense measures such as makeshift dirt mounds around its Pickaxe Mountain and Natanz nuclear sites to impede any attempted raid by ground forces.

5) On October 19, the Pentagon chief Pete Hegseth made an unannounced visit to Israel, where he met Prime Minister Benjamin Netanyahu at Ovda Air Base. The meeting also included Israeli Defense Minister Israel Katz. IDF Chief of Staff Eyal Zamir and other senior Israeli officials were reportedly not invited, for confidentiality reasons. Hegseth arrived via military transport rather than a standard US government aircraft to keep the trip low-profile. 

The new military operation against Iran might involve intense strikes targeting nuclear sites, energy infrastructure, and missile/drone arsenals as a way to force Tehran to accepting terms it has so far resisted after nearly eight months of conflict, sanctions, and the US naval blockade. Iran has refused to move enriched uranium abroad or make nuclear concessions, and it has used leverage over the Strait of Hormuz. 

It's also noting that the Iranian economy suffered severe strain due to US naval blockade of Iranian ports and intensified sanctions. Oil exports have largely collapsed, while the inflation remains extremely high. The renewed bombing campaign against energy and economic targets could be a factor that pushes the Iranian economy "over the brink" and forces the regime to make concessions.

Mehrabad airport , Iran’s main airport has been attacked . Numerous explosions seen , no reports on mainstream media . No cause explained and no group taking responsibility. Massive cargo plane with transponder off landed just before explosions occurred.

Saudi-led forces reportedly carried out airstrikes against Houthi-controlled areas in Yemen over the weekend of 24–25 October 2026. The fighting escalated as the Houthis launched missiles and drones towards Saudi Arabia.
According to reporting by Al Jazeera and other outlets, the weekend saw attacks in both directions. 
Saturday, 24 October: Reports described Saudi-led coalition airstrikes hitting areas controlled by the Houthis in Yemen, including the capital, Sanaa.
Sunday, 25 October: Saudi Arabia's coalition reported intercepting Houthi missiles and drones aimed at Riyadh and southern parts of the kingdom. 
- Casualties: Houthi-run media reported deaths and injuries from the airstrikes, including in Sanaa and Hodeidah. Those figures have not been independently verified. 
The key point: this was not just Saudi Arabia intercepting incoming missiles. Saudi-led forces were also reportedly striking Houthi positions inside Yemen, marking a further escalation 

Israeli forces carried out multiple attacks in Gaza over the last 72 hours (roughly 23–26 October 2026). Reports indicate airstrikes, drone attacks, artillery shelling and gunfire despite the ceasefire. 
Reported attacks
Sunday, 25 October — Gaza City: An Israeli strike hit the Islamic University campus. Palestinian medical officials reported 3 people killed and 8 wounded. The IDF said it targeted militants. 
Sunday, 25 October — Khan Younis: An Israeli bombardment in the al-Mawasi area reportedly killed 1 person and wounded 5. 
Sunday, 25 October — Northern and central Gaza: Reports described artillery shelling, drone strikes and gunfire in several areas, including near Hamad Hospital and north of al-Bureij. 
Friday, 23 October — Gaza City and southern Gaza: Israeli strikes reportedly killed at least 3 Palestinians, including two people targeted on a motorcycle in the al-Nasr neighbourhood and one person targeted on a bicycle near al-Mawasi, Khan Younis. 
Bottom line
Israeli military attacks in Gaza were reported on both Friday and Sunday, with multiple casualties. The reports I found do not establish a complete, independently verified casualty total for the entire 72-hour period.

hodeidah.tx:
● Reproducing claims of the Houthi militia in some media outlets, by describing them as the Yemeni government or presenting their armed formations as the Yemeni Armed Forces, contributes to misleading international public opinion and obscuring the distinction between the internationally recognized legitimate state and the militia that seized its institutions by force of arms. 
Accuracy in description is a professional and ethical responsibility, and recognizing the reality of military control over certain areas does not mean recognizing the legitimacy of state representation.

● The Iranian-backed Houthi terrorist militia speaks on behalf of Yemen and attempts to market itself to the world as the representative of the Yemeni state and the voice of the Yemeni people's will, in an effort to hijack the will of an entire people and impose its sectarian project tied to Tehran on Yemen's present and future. But its practices expose the falsehood of its claims; how can a group that bombs cities and residential neighborhoods with rockets and drones, targets civilian facilities, kills innocents in Hodeidah, Taiz, Aden, Lahj, Shabwa, Hadramaut, Marib, and other provinces, besieges cities, terrorizes women and children, and throws Yemen's sons into its wars claim to represent its victims and speak on their behalf? Yemenis are neither subjects in its racist project nor fuel for its adventures, and they have not granted it a mandate to rule them or determine their fate.

● The Republic of Yemen is a sovereign state with its constitutional institutions and internationally recognized legitimate leadership, and an armed terrorist group cannot impersonate the state or monopolize the representation of its people; legitimacy is not acquired by force of arms, nor imposed by coup and repression, but is based on the free popular will, respect for the constitution and law, protection of citizens and preservation of their dignity, and commitment to Yemen's sovereignty and the independence of its national decision. Yemen, with its Arab identity, republican history, and social and political diversity, is too great to be reduced by a militia, monopolized by a racist group, or transformed into an extension of Iranian influence.

qt.t:
The terrorist Houthi militias have shown the world what they are capable of. Their threat extends far beyond Saudi Arabia and Yemen.

In @nytopinion, I explain why the international community can no longer afford to underestimate them.

nytimes.com/2026/10/27/opi…

bab-al-mandab.tx:
🚨🇺🇸🇸🇦 In a recent New York Times opinion piece, Saudi Ambassador Reema Bandar Al-Saud @rbalsaud made a striking comparison between the fight against ISIS and the challenge posed by the terrorist Houthis:

“ISIS was defeated by local forces backed by a coalition of more than 80 nations. The Houthis can be defeated the same way. It is Yemen’s fight to lead.”

Back in 2014–2015, when ISIS was tearing through Iraq and Syria, the world didn’t just throw together a military coalition. What happened was a rare alignment of self-interest. Countries that normally disagreed on almost everything recognized that the cost of doing nothing was higher than the cost of cooperating.

The Houthis, a terrorist group, have demonstrated capabilities that pose regional and international security concerns, with Iranian support playing a significant role. They’ve launched more than a thousand ballistic missiles and drones at Saudi Arabia. They’ve threatened the Bab al-Mandab Strait, a critical chokepoint for global trade. Their activities have also raised concerns about weapons proliferation, regional militancy, and the recruitment and indoctrination of children.

A disruption to Saudi energy production or export routes could raise fuel, transport, and manufacturing costs worldwide, feeding inflation and squeezing households and businesses far beyond the region.

With ISIS, the death toll and refugee waves hit European and American communities hard enough to force the issue. Much of the human cost of the Houthi threat, by contrast, has fallen on Yemenis and Saudis, while many foreign capitals continue to treat it as a regional problem.

She’s not just saying we need another coalition of more than 80 nations. She’s pointing to a lesson from the fight against ISIS: international cooperation becomes possible when enough countries recognize that the threat extends beyond any single region.

By the time a major disruption to shipping drives up prices for consumers in Chicago or Hamburg, or advances in missile technology create a more immediate threat to distant countries, the cost of responding could be much higher.

Saudi Arabia is working with Yemeni partners, helping counter weapons smuggling, restricting financial channels, and providing humanitarian assistance. Countries should designate the Houthis as a terrorist organization, cut off their funding, intercept weapons shipments at sea, and strengthen support for Yemen’s legitimate government.

Saudi Arabia has a legitimate interest in defending its people and territory and preventing Yemen from becoming a permanent platform for cross-border attacks and regional instability. At the same time, lasting security cannot be built on military pressure alone. It requires a viable Yemeni state, functioning institutions, humanitarian relief, and a political future in which Yemenis, not armed factions backed by outside powers, determine their country’s direction.

Any effective response must be coordinated, grounded in international law, attentive to civilian protection, and paired with a credible path toward peace.

Saudi Arabia should not have to wait for the rest of the world to feel the danger before that danger is acknowledged.

Saudi Arabia’s security, regional security, Yemen’s stability, global energy security, and the freedom of international navigation are inseparable parts of that challenge.

PEACE IS NEVER SECURED BY IGNORING THE THREAT.

bab-al-mandab.tx:
I've seen a lot of discussion lately about the Strait of Hormuz losing relevance. To put it plainly, that is a short-sighted opinion that has no supporting evidence.

Flows and loadings are irrelevant if the product can't get to where it is going and where it is going is Asia. 80-90% of all crude exports from the Middle East/Gulf region are destined for Asia. 

There is no amount of bypassing, re-routing, or pipelines that is going to avoid that oil having to pass through either the Strait of Hormuz or the Bab al-Mandab. 

I'm not even going to seriously consider the idea of loading at Yanbu, transiting the Suez Canal (utilizing Sumed), through the Mediterranean, down the Atlantic, around the Cape of Good Hope and into the Indian Ocean on to Asian markets. 

That is a workaround that is only available to Saudi Arabia and it is absolutely not sustainable. Freight rates would be even higher than they are now with Iran shooting at ships. It'd be cheaper for Saudi Arabia to pay Iran off. The Cape of Good Hope is a break glass in case some moron gets his ship stuck in the Suez Canal option, not a sustainable long-term alternative.

Yes, in a perfect world there is a Saudi-UAE-Oman pipeline that bypasses the Strait and outputs directly to the Arabian Sea at Duqm or Ras Markaz. Earlier this month Saudi Arabia began a feasibility study for such a pipeline, but that study is going to come to the same conclusion as every study prior. It isn't feasible.

It would be cost-prohibitive, the terrain and climate are hell on earth, there is no logistical infrastructure in place to even support such a pipeline, and the political obstacles (like who would control it) would be insurmountable. It would also be well within range of drones and ballistic missiles from both Iran and Ansarallah.

So yes, while the total crude oil exports have been able to successfully shift ~20% around the Strait, at the end of the day most of that oil still has to pass through one of two major chokepoints to get to its final destination and right now neither of those chokepoints is under firm control.

Ultimately this isn't a new problem. These choke points have existed for thousands of years. If there were a viable and affordable alternative option, it would have presented itself long before now. This isn't the first time there has been a tanker war, after all.

suez.t: In October 1943, Germany was losing the war on every front. But at the behest of the Grand Mufti, Luftwaffe intelligence officers were studying how to bomb Tel…
suez.tx:
In October 1943, Germany was losing the war on every front. But at the behest of the Grand Mufti, Luftwaffe intelligence officers were studying how to bomb Tel Aviv.

Their assessment considered the city “the citadel of Palestinian Jewry and émigré Jews.” Unlike Jerusalem, whose population was a little more than half Jewish and which contained Christian and Muslim holy sites, Tel Aviv was nearly 100% Jewish. The Nazis determined that bombing there would kill the maximum number of Jews. Officers noted that the city had no major military installations of value. The point was not strategic advantage, but to kill Jews.

The idea had been pushed by Amin al-Husseini, who was then in Berlin collaborating with the Nazis. He and others had repeatedly asked for attacks on Tel Aviv. Earlier in the summer of 1943, a similar proposal reached Hermann Göring and was rejected because the Luftwaffe no longer had any long-range capacity to spare. Yet the intelligence section still produced a detailed demographic and targeting study.

One officer, First Lieutenant Zetsche, discussed a possible symbolic raid on the Jewish Agency building in Jerusalem around the anniversary of the Balfour Declaration, while acknowledging that Jerusalem itself offered no military importance. The preferred option remained Tel Aviv because it maximized Jewish casualties.

The plan never advanced to an attack since, by late 1943, the Luftwaffe lacked the forces to carry out the raid and Germany’s position in the Mediterranean had collapsed. But the existence of the study shows that, even in retreat, some Nazi planners continued to treat the murder of Jewish civilians in Mandate Palestine as an aspirational objective.

Earlier in the war, an Einsatzgruppe had been prepared to exterminate the Jews of Mandate Palestine in the event of an Axis advance beyond the Suez Canal. When that front failed at the Battle of El Alamein, aerial bombardment was one of the remaining options under discussion.

The fact that the assessment was written by Luftwaffe intelligence officers, not the SS, makes the antisemitic reasoning especially clear: they openly weighed which city would kill the most Jews.

suez.t: On this day—October 23, 1942 An SS Einsatzkommando unit was waiting in Athens for the order to bring the Holocaust to Mandate Palestine’s Jews when British for…
suez.tx:
On this day—October 23, 1942

An SS Einsatzkommando unit was waiting in Athens for the order to bring the Holocaust to Mandate Palestine’s Jews when British forces under Montgomery opened the Second Battle of El Alamein.

By the summer of 1942, Erwin Rommel’s Afrika Korps had driven deep into Egypt. British forces held a defensive line at El Alamein, 60 miles west of Alexandria. From there, the road to the Suez Canal and to Mandate Palestine with nearly 600,000 Jews was open. Another 75,000 lived in Egypt, and both communities understood the danger. Reports of mass killings of Jews in Europe had already reached them.

In Berlin, an Einsatzkommando under Walther Rauff was assembled and positioned in Athens. Its orders were to carry out “special operations” against the Jewish population once Axis forces advanced beyond Egypt. Local Arabs in Mandate Palestine, anticipating a German arrival, marked Jewish houses for seizure. Grandi Mufti Amin al-Husseini had already met with Hitler and sought Arab units to fight alongside German forces against the Jews and the British.

On the night of October 23, Montgomery’s Eighth Army launched a massive artillery barrage and infantry assault. Over the following days, the Axis lines broke. Rommel’s forces began a long retreat to the west. The Einsatzkommando never deployed to Mandate Palestine, but it later operated in Tunisia.

The battle is usually remembered as a turning point in the North African campaign. For the Jews of Mandate Palestine and Egypt, it was the point at which a planned extension of the Holocaust was halted.

suez.t: October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts in…
suez.tx:
October 23, 1942. At twenty minutes to ten at night, in the desert of Egypt, more than eight hundred British guns open fire at once, and the darkness erupts into a wall of flame and thunder that can be felt in the chest from miles away. The Second Battle of El Alamein has begun. It is the battle that will finally break Rommel in the desert, the hinge of the whole war in North Africa, and the victory that Churchill would say marked "the end of the beginning."

I have been following the desert war since the early days of this series, Rommel the Desert Fox running the British ragged back and forth across Libya and Egypt, the see-saw campaign that had swung all the way to El Alamein, the last defensible line before the Nile, the Suez Canal, and the oil of the Middle East. In the summer Rommel had been stopped there, barely, in the first battle. Now the British Eighth Army had a new commander, Bernard Montgomery, a careful, methodical, supremely confident general who had rebuilt the army's morale and refused to attack until he had overwhelming strength.

And by October he had it. Montgomery had built up a crushing superiority, in men, in tanks, in guns, in aircraft, in supplies, far more than Rommel could match, because the Axis supply line across the Mediterranean was being strangled while the British were pouring reinforcements, including masses of new American-built Sherman tanks, into Egypt. Rommel himself was away sick in Germany when the blow fell, his army dug in behind vast belts of mines and wire the Germans grimly called the "Devil's Gardens."

Montgomery's plan was not clever maneuver but deliberate, grinding attrition, a battle he called "crumbling." It opened on the night of the 23rd with one of the greatest artillery bombardments since the First World War, those eight hundred-plus guns firing in a stupendous barrage that announced the offensive and smashed at the Axis positions. Then the infantry went in, in the moonlight, to clear paths through the enormous minefields so the armor could pass, and the fighting settled into a brutal, close-quarters slog through the mines and the dug-in defenses.

It was not quick. For days the battle hung in the balance, the British grinding forward yard by yard through the Devil's Gardens, taking heavy losses, the attack at times seeming to stall. Rommel rushed back from Germany to take command, but he had no answer to Montgomery's material superiority and his relentless pressure, and critically he was running out of fuel, his tanks increasingly immobilized for lack of petrol. Montgomery kept up the attrition, wearing the Axis forces down, destroying tanks he could replace and Rommel could not, until at last, in early November, he concentrated his armor and punched through.

Rommel's front broke. Against Hitler's furious orders to stand and die, Rommel, to save what was left of his army, began a long retreat westward across the desert, a withdrawal that would not stop for hundreds of miles. The Axis army in the desert had been decisively beaten for the first time, and it would never recover the initiative. Combined with the Anglo-American landings in northwest Africa that came just days later, El Alamein doomed the entire Axis position in North Africa.

The victory meant an enormous amount, and not just militarily. It was the first great, clear-cut British land victory over the Germans in the whole war, coming after years of defeats and retreats, and it was desperately needed for Allied morale. Church bells were rung in Britain to celebrate. Churchill captured its meaning in one of his famous lines: "Now this is not the end. It is not even the beginning of the end. But it is, perhaps, the end of the beginning." The tide in the west had turned, and it turned here, in the desert, beginning with those eight hundred guns firing into the dark on the night of the 23rd.

suez.tx:
Mohammad Ali al-Houthi, member of Ansarallah's Supreme Political Council, criticized Saudi Arabia's claims of seeking regional de-escalation through its defense minister's visit to Tehran, arguing that Riyadh's diplomatic rhetoric contradicts its continued war, blockade, and occupation of Yemen.
——
In a statement responding to the Saudi Foreign Ministry, al-Houthi outlined the following positions:

• Riyadh cannot claim to promote regional peace and security while continuing its military attacks, blockade, and occupation of Yemen. Houthi said Saudi Arabia's actions directly contradict its stated commitment to de-escalation.

• Saudi Arabia must halt its aggression, lift the blockade, withdraw from occupied Yemeni territory, and compensate Yemen for destruction caused since 2015. He stressed that if Saudi attacks cease, Yemeni operations will also stop and normal life can resume.

• Houthi criticized the so-called 'Mecca Defense Pact', arguing that it seeks to address what its members call the Iranian crisis while concealing what he described as outright aggression against Iran. He warned that Saudi Arabia's previous alliances had failed and that Riyadh had even turned against former partners.

• He condemned Egypt and its parliament for supporting the defense of Saudi Arabia, arguing that such a position effectively amounts to declaring war on Yemen. He warned that Egypt risks repeating its military entanglement in Yemen during the 1960s, exhausting its forces and potentially leaving Sinai vulnerable to Israeli expansion and plans to displace Palestinians into Egyptian territory.

• Houthi stressed that Yemen does not fear new military alliances but warned these countries against supporting Saudi attacks, the blockade, or the occupation of Yemen. He urged them instead to direct their cooperation against Israel, which he said is waging war across Palestine, Lebanon, Syria, and Iran while also threatening Egypt.

• He rejected claims that Yemen poses a threat to regional waterways, maintaining that Yemen's position contributes to protecting Bab al-Mandab, the Suez Canal, and the wider Arab and Islamic region.

• He reaffirmed that Yemen's political and military position has remained unchanged since 2015, arguing that US, British, and Israeli intelligence agencies manufacture fears of unspecified threats to perpetuate divisions and conflict within the Arab and Islamic world.

taiwan-strait.t: Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?” It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the G…
taiwan-strait.tx:
Gideon Rachman asks whether the world is “sleepwalking into World War III?”

It’s a long read, and not a terribly enlightening one. Rachman tours Ukraine, the Gulf, the Taiwan Strait and the 65 conflicts currently raging around the world, and finds the culprits to be “revisionist powers”, “strongman leaders” and an “axis of adversaries”: Russia, China, Iran and North Korea.

In a couple of thousand words, he finds no space at all for the crisis of neoliberal capitalism, albeit he does note the important fact that the G7, which accounted for two-thirds of world output in 1989, is now down to 43 percent.

Lenin would have recognised the connection between this decline and the attempt by declining powers to use military means to hold on to a world they can no longer dominate economically. He would have easily recognised “the striving for domination, not for freedom”.

More than a century after his death, Lenin remains a far better and more relevant guide to the questions of war and peace than the FT’s chief foreign affairs commentator.

Imperialism is hitting out in all directions:

• Genocide in Gaza, armed and financed by Washington, London and Berlin.

• US-Israeli criminal war on Iran and Lebanon.

• A proxy war in Ukraine to weaken and dismember Russia.

• Economic warfare against China: tariffs, chip bans, sanctions, blacklists.

• A “Donroe Doctrine” under which a president is kidnapped, Cuba is placed under a genocidal energy siege, and election results are determined in Washington DC.

• AUKUS, RIMPAC, Talisman Sabre, and a ring of US bases around China’s coast.

None of this features as a cause of insecurity in Rachman’s telling. He’s more worried about whether Xi Jinping “considers that America’s Taiwan Relations Act means something”, or whether Putin sees NATO’s Article Five as an “iconclad commitment”.

In other words, his proposed path to peace is for the US to make its threats more credible. Peace through NATO. Peace through imperialism.

The real guarantee of peace is a multipolar world where no power gets to dictate terms to the rest – exactly what Rachman’s “axis of adversaries” is working towards, and exactly what the West is fighting to prevent.

taiwan-strait.tx:
🇺🇸 TODAY IN AMERICAN HISTORY: THE TRAGIC FINAL MISSION OF THE USS TANG

October 24, 1944 — 82 years ago today.

The USS Tang (SS-306) was one of America’s most successful submarines during World War II.

Under the command of Lieutenant Commander Richard H. O’Kane, Tang carried out five combat patrols against Japanese shipping in the Pacific.

During her final patrol, Tang attacked a Japanese convoy in the Taiwan Strait.

But tragedy struck.

ONE OF HER OWN TORPEDOES CIRCLED BACK AND HIT THE SUBMARINE!

Tang sank in approximately 180 feet of water.

Of the 87 American sailors aboard, only nine survived.

Some of the survivors escaped from the submerged submarine using emergency escape equipment, an extraordinary feat under terrifying conditions.

Those who survived were captured by Japanese forces and held as prisoners of war.

Commander O’Kane survived and later received the Medal of Honor.

78 AMERICAN SAILORS NEVER CAME HOME.

Their courage and sacrifice deserve to be remembered.

🇺🇸 Fair winds and following seas, gentlemen. Your sacrifice will never be forgotten.

ras-laffan.tx:
🇶🇦 QatarEnergy has lined up 3 US deals in 2 days.

The world’s second-largest LNG exporter is now buying American LNG.

Cheniere Energy, Inc.: signed, 4m tonnes a year from 2031 to 2054

Venture Global LNG: in advanced talks for at least 3m tonnes a year

Woodside Energy’s Louisiana LNG: in talks for up to 3m tonnes a year over 15–20 years

If all 3 close, that’s about 10m tonnes a year. 

Add Qatar’s 70% of the 18m-tonne Golden Pass plant in Texas ( ExxonMobil).

Why would Qatar buy gas from someone else?

Because this year a single strait cut off its exports.

When Hormuz shut, QatarEnergy declared force majeure and bought 33 spot cargoes of US LNG, mostly from Venture Global, to keep supplying Korea, Taiwan, India and Japan.

In LNG your reputation depends on delivering. 

Qatar’s customers have 20-year contracts with it. 

If it can’t ship from Ras Laffan, it ships from Louisiana.

Then there’s the price.

Many of Qatar’s long-term Asian contracts are linked to crude oil. 

US LNG costs about 115% of Henry Hub plus a liquefaction fee of around $2.50. 

With Henry Hub near $3, that’s about $6 at the plant before shipping.

So Qatar can buy at a Henry Hub price and sell at an oil-linked price.

Qatar doesn’t set the oil price, but every extra dollar on Brent lifts what its oil-linked buyers pay.

Every US cargo Qatar buys is a cargo Europe and Asia can’t. 

The world’s biggest LNG seller is now bidding against its own customers for American supply.

That’s why JKM and TTF sit near $30.

Qatar is buying a second route out and Henry Hub is starting to shape prices in Doha.

American #naturalgas isn't a short-lived "bridge fuel." It's the backbone of global energy security, and the world's buyers are voting with their checkbooks.

qt.t:
The US doing a major military escalation against Iran with just 13 days left until the midterms has massive risks for Trump.

No, this is not related to the economic impact of disrupting oil or anything like that.

There's a much more Carter-esque possibility here.

What the US is talking about is a "short, intense campaign" against Iranian infrastructure & likely nuclear facilities.

On more than one occasion in April, Iranian air defenses shot down manned US aircraft. This was after weeks of intense bombardment of air defenses to the point that they were deemed largely gone.

Ever since July, Iran has rapidly been upgrading & rebuilding its air defenses. They are almost certainly stronger than they were back in April in the midst of the heaviest period of joint US-Israeli bombardment.

While it is possible to shoot down a plane at any point, the most likely time would be when Iranian air defenses are most intact & there are the highest number of targets in the air. In this case, the beginning of a new escalation.

There is a significant, non trivial chance a manned aircraft will be shot down. Again, this isn't some questionable Iranian boast, it happened earlier in the war.

Last

ras-laffan.tx:
The idea that more intense kinetic escalation will lead to a clean, quick outcome where Iran surrenders (before or after the midterms) is foolish.

This has been tried multiple times & each time results in a *more* aggressive Iran that lashes out with less restraint.

Is there extreme pain for the Iranian people & lasting damage to the country?

Yes.

Does it result in the Islamic Republic backing down?

Not at all. They don't care.

And the less they have to lose, the more extreme they get. The reason Iran has restrained from extensive strikes on vital regional infrastructure is because it is worried of mutual assured destruction & its own infrastructure getting hit.

If you're going to hit power plants and dams anyway then that restraint goes away.

With every step, Netanyahu & his sadistic zealots at the FDD have lied to Trump that "just one more step" will lead to the end of Iran problem.

This started with assassinations of individuals, small military campaigns, more extreme sanctions, and eventually a 12 day war & a 7 month war.

Yet neither killing Khamenei nor hitting Fordow made the problem go away. There was always magically more work to be done. And additional, more extreme strikes needed.

In response to these actions Iran went from symbolic, coordinated strikes to shooting medium range ballistic missiles in Israeli cities to eventually the destruction of multiple US bases, actually closing the Strait of Hormuz, and even hitting Ras Laffan gas fields (something with global repercussions).

History shows that:

- Yes Israel & the US will be able to get some tactical achievements
- They will not be able to get a strategic victory and the conflict will continue
- Iran will react with a massive escalation that was previously considered too extreme
- There will not be a quick ending
- The US will eventually try to calm things down because the escalations are getting too uncomfortable and things go into a period of relative calm until the cycle is repeated again.

Typically during the periods of relative calm between escalations the US is able to do more sustained damage through economic pressure & the Iranian response is relatively restrained. But the kinetic escalations always lead to unexpected extreme results.

It's very stupid and very risky & any other US president but Trump would not continue to listen to the insane fanatics pushing him that way for yet another round.

Mumbai’s aviation landscape is gearing up for a major shift as IndiGo and Air India Group expand at Adani Airports operated Navi Mumbai International Airport (NMIA).

IndiGo plans to move 12 daily international departures to NMIA between February and July 2027, covering Bahrain, Riyadh, Dammam, Jeddah, Madinah, Kuwait, Ras Al Khaimah, Fujairah, Muscat, Dhaka and Jakarta. Daily Kathmandu flights will take its network to 12 international destinations.

Air India Express plans 4 daily domestic flights from December 2026, followed by Oman and planned Kuwait services from January 2027. Its West Asia transition includes Jeddah, Riyadh, Dammam, Doha, Muscat and Sharjah.

Adani Airports is coordinating the phased transition to strengthen connectivity and support CSMIA Terminal 1 redevelopment by 2030.
